The Story of Gopvati

I bow to Lord Jina, praised and glorified by the world and the giver of all happiness, and I write the story of Gopvati, which awakens the feeling of renunciation in the heart.

In the village of Palas lived an ordinary householder named Sinhbhal. His wife was Gopvati, a woman of wicked nature. Through her constant quarrelling day and night, poor Sinhbhal's life was ruined. Not once, even for a moment, did Gopvati ever give him any happiness.

Wearied by Gopvati, Sinhbhal went one day to a nearby village called Padminikhet. There, without telling anyone, he secretly married Subhadra, the beautiful daughter of Sinhsen Chaudhary. Somehow Gopvati learned of this. Upon hearing the news, she was consumed with rage. She could not bear Sinhbhal's transgression and began plotting to punish him for it.

One evening, around seven o'clock, Gopvati left her house and walked to Padminikhet, arriving around eleven at night. She went straight to Sinhsen's house. The family assumed she had come on some urgent business and would explain in the morning, so they went to sleep. Gopvati also lay down, pretending to sleep. But when everyone was deep in slumber, she crept silently to the room where poor Subhadra lay sleeping beside her mother. The wicked woman cut off Subhadra's head and carried it home in the darkness of night.

At dawn, Sinhbhal learned of the terrible deed. Seeing Subhadra's lifeless body, he was overwhelmed with grief. He returned to his own home with a heavy heart. Upon seeing him, Gopvati began treating him with great respect and affection, serving him food with every show of love. But Sinhbhal's heart was pierced so deeply by Subhadra's death that nothing could please him, and he remained perpetually sorrowful. And truly, what pleasure can food hold for one who is deeply grieving?

Seeing Sinhbhal's grief for Subhadra, Gopvati's fury only increased. One day, as the wretched man sat eating in sorrow, Gopvati brought Subhadra's severed head and placed it upon his plate, saying, "Yes, without seeing this you found no pleasure in your meal — now surely you will enjoy it!"

At the sight of Subhadra's head on his plate, Sinhbhal's heart shattered utterly. In that moment of extreme horror, all attachment to worldly life left him. He saw the true nature of existence — how cruel, how fleeting, how filled with suffering. He renounced the world entirely, became a monk, and devoted himself to the path of liberation. Through deep meditation and austere penance, he eventually purified his soul and attained moksha.

This story teaches that the world is full of cruelty, attachment, and horror. Those who cling to worldly bonds invite only suffering. But even from the depths of horror, the soul can awaken to renunciation. Sinhbhal's terrible loss became the catalyst for his liberation — proving that when worldly illusion is shattered, the path to truth opens at last.
